The salt spray didn’t just wet Elias; it stung him. For forty years, he had stood watch at the edge of the world, where the Atlantic churned against the jagged teeth of Blackwood Rock. His days were measured in rotations of the great Fresnel lens, a rhythmic heartbeat of light cutting through the fog. The lighthouse was not a home, but a fortress against the dark, and Elias was its sole guardian.

One November night, the wind howled like a wounded animal. The storm had swallowed the horizon, turning the sea into a churning void of black and white. Elias climbed the spiral stairs, his knees protesting the age that had crept in like rust. Inside the lantern room, the air was thick with the smell of kerosene and ozone. He checked the oil, polished the glass until it gleamed like a diamond, and lit the wick. The beam swept out, a golden sword slicing through the tempest.
